preamble: Fricativization of the close back rounded vowel [u] to the labiodental fricative [f]. Cappadocian Greek shows a generally acknowledged case in the plural of 'ear': earlier ta otjá > ta utjá > ta ftjá, from which a new singular to ftí was formed. Janse & Vandewalle (2020) argue the same high-vowel fricativization in ta ušáxja > ta fšáxja 'the children', though they also offer an alternative etymology for fšáx.

examples.note: Unstressed [u] became [f] before voiceless [t]; the singular to ftí 'the ear' was then made by back-formation.
Sg. to fšáx 'child' (Pharasiot fšáxi 'boy') by metanalysis; Janse & Vandewalle also consider an origin from Old Turkish uvşak 'little'.

sources: Janse, M., & Vandewalle, J. (2020). The history and etymology of Cappadocian fšáx 'child', Pharasiot fšáxi 'boy'. Transactions of the Philological Society 118(3), 500–514. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-968X.12202
